steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on using large language models to rewrite long-tail queries in Taobao's e-commerce search. Explain the semantic gap problem, go over prior approaches to query rewriting, present our three-stage fine-tuning framework, and finish with a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- E-commerce search and the semantic gap for long-tail queries
- Prior work: embedding-based retrieval, discriminative and generative query rewriting, LLM-based augmentation
- Our framework \method: three stages of fine-tuning an LLM
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- E-commerce search and the semantic gap
  - rapid growth of e-commerce; Taobao, JD, Amazon: hundreds of millions of users, billions of GMV annually
  - search paradigm (Figure 1): "semantic understanding - retrieval - rank"
  - semantic understanding = foundation, accurate matching of user intent
  - users express preferences differently -> semantic gap between queries and product keywords; worse for long-tail queries, maybe no relevant products at all
  - example: "self-building blind box" vs synonymous "DIY blind box"; inverted index can't match "DIY" with non-customary "self-building"
  - need to solve semantic gap for long-tail queries, the “ \nothing ” problem
- Prior work
  - embedding based retrieval (cite): common semantic space, Top- K retrieval with ANN; outcomes hard to interpret -> limits performance
  - “query rewriting & exact match” for controllability
  - discriminative (cite): similar terms from query reformulation set + sparse retrieval; fine for hot queries, long-tail not optimized, no related rewrite
  - generative (cite): supervised training on <query, rewrite> pairs; alignment (cite) for metric preference; small generative models, limited comprehension of long-tail
  - LLMs as retrieval data augmentation generators, no training (cite); even with curated prompts, poor specialization / alignment with e-commerce objectives
- \method
  - three stages: multi-instruction SFT, offline system feedback, objective alignment
  - stage 1: rejection sampling for <query, rewrite> pairs with desired quality distribution; plus quality classification, product title prediction, CoT tasks -> multi-instruction rewriting dataset
  - stage 2: beam search -> multiple candidate rewrites; Taobao offline system retrieves products; quality score of retrieved products = rewards for ranking candidates
  - stage 3: Bradley-Terry based contrastive learning, partial order among rewrites, calibrates generation probability
  - training objective aligned with online goal of Taobao search
- Contributions
  - analyzed long-tail queries, identified semantic gap; first to fine-tune LLMs for industrial query rewriting
  - three-stage framework \method, rewrites aligned with Taobao search objectives
  - offline and online experiments; significant improvement in e-commerce revenue

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
E-commerce platforms have grown very fast in the past decades. Big e-commerce companies like Taobao, JD and Amazon have hundreds of millions of users and billions of gross merchandise volume (GMV) every year. To help these users retrieve related products quickly, a well-established search paradigm has been proposed, shown in Figure 1. This paradigm has several steps, i.e., “semantic understanding - retrieval - rank”. Semantic understanding is the foundation of the whole system, and it makes sure user intent is matched accurately. But users express their preferences for products in different ways, so there are often semantic gaps between their queries and the product keywords. This is even worse for long-tail queries, where the retrieval system may not give any relevant products at all. For example, a user with personal expression habits may type a long-tail query like "self-building blind box", and this would get more retrieval results if it was the synonymous query "DIY blind box". Traditional term-matching solutions like inverted index will probably fail to match the commonly-used “DIY” with the non-customary term “self-building”, which limits the retrieval results and hurts the user experience a lot. So we urgently need to solve the semantic gap challenge for long-tail queries and address the problem of “ \nothing ” in e-commerce platform.

Prior work mostly focuses on the “embedding based retrieval” paradigm. These methods first map queries and products into a common semantic space and then do Top- K retrieval with approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) methods. The problem is that the retrieval outcomes can be hard to interpret, and this severely limits the performance. To make the retrieval outcomes more controllable, some work has been done on the “query rewriting & exact match” paradigm. The discriminative methods try to “rewrite” queries by finding similar terms from a query reformulation set, and then use these terms to search for relevant products with sparse retrieval. These approaches can expand the semantic of hot queries well, but long-tail queries may not be optimized enough, so no related rewrite can be generated for them. The generative methods do supervised training on <query, rewrite> pair data so that the model gets rewriting capabilities, and an alignment process is also added to enhance the metric preference. These methods partly address the semantic gap problem, but they usually rely on small generative models that have limited comprehension of long-tail queries, and this constrains the rewriting capability a lot. Recently, as LLM techniques developed, some work uses LLMs only as retrieval data augmentation generators, without additional training, to expand query semantics. But even with carefully curated prompts, these methods may still limit the ability to specialize for the query rewriting task, which leads to poor alignment with the objectives of e-commerce search.

- \method: three stages of fine-tuning LLMs
  - multi-instruction SFT, offline system feedback, objective alignment
  - stage 1: rejection sampling for <query, rewrite> pairs with desired quality distribution; combine with quality classification, product title prediction and CoT tasks -> multi-instruction rewriting dataset
  - stage 2: beam search -> candidate rewrites -> Taobao offline system -> quality score of retrieved products as rewards for ranking
  - Bradley-Terry based contrastive learning on partial order of rewrites to calibrate generation probability
  - objective aligned with online goal of Taobao search
- Contributions
  - analyzed long-tail queries, semantic gap; first to fine-tune LLMs for industrial query rewriting
  - three-stage framework \method aligned with Taobao search objectives
  - offline + online experiments, significant e-commerce revenue improvement

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
E-commerce platforms have grown very fast in the past decades. Big e-commerce companies like Taobao, JD and Amazon have hundreds of millions of users and billions of gross merchandise volume (GMV) every year. To help these users retrieve related products quickly, a well-established search paradigm has been proposed, shown in Figure 1. This paradigm has several steps, i.e., “semantic understanding - retrieval - rank”. Semantic understanding is the foundation of the whole system, and it makes sure user intent is matched accurately. But users express their preferences for products in different ways, so there are often semantic gaps between their queries and the product keywords. This is even worse for long-tail queries, where the retrieval system may not give any relevant products at all. For example, a user with personal expression habits may type a long-tail query like "self-building blind box", and this would get more retrieval results if it was the synonymous query "DIY blind box". Traditional term-matching solutions like inverted index will probably fail to match the commonly-used “DIY” with the non-customary term “self-building”, which limits the retrieval results and hurts the user experience a lot. So we urgently need to solve the semantic gap challenge for long-tail queries and address the problem of “ \nothing ” in e-commerce platform.

Prior work mostly focuses on the “embedding based retrieval” paradigm. These methods first map queries and products into a common semantic space and then do Top- K retrieval with approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) methods. The problem is that the retrieval outcomes can be hard to interpret, and this severely limits the performance. To make the retrieval outcomes more controllable, some work has been done on the “query rewriting & exact match” paradigm. The discriminative methods try to “rewrite” queries by finding similar terms from a query reformulation set, and then use these terms to search for relevant products with sparse retrieval. These approaches can expand the semantic of hot queries well, but long-tail queries may not be optimized enough, so no related rewrite can be generated for them. The generative methods do supervised training on <query, rewrite> pair data so that the model gets rewriting capabilities, and an alignment process is also added to enhance the metric preference. These methods partly address the semantic gap problem, but they usually rely on small generative models that have limited comprehension of long-tail queries, and this constrains the rewriting capability a lot. Recently, as LLM techniques developed, some work uses LLMs only as retrieval data augmentation generators, without additional training, to expand query semantics. But even with carefully curated prompts, these methods may still limit the ability to specialize for the query rewriting task, which leads to poor alignment with the objectives of e-commerce search.

We propose \method to bridge the semantic gap for long-tail queries and solve the above challenges, by producing controlled and aligned outcomes while integrating the knowledge of LLMs. \method is a novel framework with three stages of fine-tuning LLMs: multi-instruction supervised fine-tuning (SFT), offline system feedback, and objective alignment. In the first stage, we use rejection sampling to collect <query, rewrite> pairs with the desired quality distribution. Then we combine these pairs with data from quality classification, product title prediction and chain of thought (CoT) tasks to build the multi-instruction rewriting dataset, and we fine-tune our LLM on it. Next, we use the well-trained LLM with beam search to generate multiple candidate rewrites for each query. The candidate rewrites are fed into the Taobao offline system, which retrieves a collection of related products. We calculate the quality score of the retrieved products for the rewrites and use the scores as rewards for ranking the candidates. To calibrate the generation probability of the candidate rewrites, we introduce a Bradley-Terry based contrastive learning method that considers the partial order among these rewrites. In the end the model training objective is aligned with the online goal of the Taobao search, so the generated rewrites give the desired search results.

Our main contributions are as follows:

- • We analyzed long-tail queries in e-commerce search and found the semantic gap problem for these queries. As far as we know, we are the first to fine-tune LLMs for an industrial query rewriting task.

- • We propose a three-stage fine-tuned framework, \method, to address the semantic gap in long-tail queries. The framework is designed to generate rewrites that align with the objectives of Taobao search.

- • We show the effectiveness of our model with both offline and online experiments, and it can significantly improve e-commerce revenue.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Past decades have seen the rapid growth of e-commerce platforms. Leading e-commerce companies, such as Taobao, JD and Amazon, have amassed hundreds of millions of users, generating billions of gross merchandise volume (GMV) annually. To facilitate the quick retrieval of related products for these users, a well-established search paradigm has been proposed, as illustrated in Figure 1. This paradigm involves several steps, i.e., “semantic understanding - retrieval - rank”. Among them, semantic understanding serves as the foundation of the entire system, ensuring accurate matching of user intent. However, because users vary in how they express their preferences for products, semantic gaps often exist between their queries and the product keywords, and this is even worse with long-tail queries, where the retrieval system may fail to provide any relevant products. For instance, a user with personal expression habits may input a long-tail query like "self-building blind box", which would lead to more retrieval results with its synonymous query "DIY blind box". Unfortunately, traditional term-matching solutions like inverted index will probably fail to match the commonly-used “DIY” with the non-customary term “self-building”, which limits the retrieval results and significantly impairs the user experience. Therefore, it is urgent to solve the semantic gap challenge for long-tail queries and address the problem of “ \nothing ” in e-commerce platform.

Traditionally, prior arts [1,2,3,4] mainly focus on the “embedding based retrieval” paradigm, which first maps the queries and products into a common semantic space and then supports Top- K retrieval with approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) methods. However, the retrieval outcomes can be difficult to interpret, which severely limits the performance. To enhance the controllability of retrieval outcomes, some efforts have been made on the “query rewriting & exact match” paradigm. On the one hand, the discriminative methods [5,6] attempt to “rewrite” queries by finding similar terms from a query reformulation set, and then use them to search for relevant products using sparse retrieval. Although these approaches can effectively expand the semantic of hot queries, long-tail queries may not be adequately optimized, so no related rewrite can be generated. On the other hand, the generative methods [7,8] involve supervised training on <query, rewrite> pair data to give the model rewriting capabilities, and an alignment process [9,10] is further incorporated to enhance the metric preference. Although these methods partially address the semantic gap problem, they typically rely on small generative models with limited comprehension of long-tail queries, which significantly constrains the rewriting capability. Recently, with the development of LLM techniques, some efforts [11,12,13,14] use LLMs solely as retrieval data augmentation generators, without additional training, to expand query semantics. However, even with carefully curated prompts, these methods may still be constrained in their ability to specialize for the query rewriting task, leading to poor alignment with the objectives of e-commerce search.

To effectively bridge the semantic gap for long-tail queries, and to solve the above challenges by producing controlled and aligned outcomes that integrate the knowledge of LLMs, we propose \method, a novel framework that involves three stages of fine-tuning LLMs, namely multi-instruction supervised fine-tuning (SFT), offline system feedback, and objective alignment. Specifically, in the first stage, we use rejection sampling to collect <query, rewrite> pairs with a desired quality distribution, and then combine these pairs with data from quality classification, product title prediction and chain of thought (CoT) tasks to construct the multi-instruction rewriting dataset for fine-tuning our LLM. Next, with the well-trained LLM, we employ beam search to generate multiple candidate rewrites for each query. These candidate rewrites are fed into the Taobao offline system to retrieve a collection of related products. We calculate the quality score of the retrieved products for the rewrites and use them as rewards for ranking the candidates. To calibrate the generation probability of the candidate rewrites, we introduce a Bradley-Terry based contrastive learning method that considers the partial order among these rewrites. Ultimately, the model training objective is aligned with the online goal of the Taobao search, ensuring that the generated rewrites yield the desired search results.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

- • We have analyzed long-tail queries in e-commerce search and identified the semantic gap problem associated with them. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to fine-tune LLMs for an industrial query rewriting task.

- • We propose a three-stage fine-tuned framework called \method to address the semantic gap in long-tail queries. The framework is designed to generate rewrites that align with the objectives of Taobao search.

- • We demonstrate the effectiveness of our model through both offline and online experiments, showing that it significantly improves e-commerce revenue.
